#8220. The Boyhood Deer Hunt That Turned Jim Carmichel Into a Gun Guy

Black Friday deals are here — Shop hunting gear, fishing tackle, optics, and more!

Published Nov 26, 2026 6:00 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

When I was a skinny, big-footed kid in grammar school, I had the unbelievably good luck of being yanked out of school for several days to go on a deer-hunting vacation with my family. Nowadays, thanks to the game commission’s deer stocking and management programs, deer are plentiful in the mountains of east Tennessee, but in the 1940s they were nonexistent. That meant that going on a real deer hunt involved traveling hundreds of miles and visiting places as far removed from our farm as was the back side of the moon. It was, to my mind, an elegant adventure, sort of like going to Europe or taking an ocean cruise. Nothing could be finer. My chums were green with envy.

Our hosts were old family friends who had struck it rich and bought an historic plantation in Virginia, complete with antebellum mansion and miles of sweet-scented hardwood forest.

On the day we arrived, dressed in our Sunday best, in a gleaming pickup truck, our host had shot a nice buck and it hung in the smokehouse. I remember inspecting the animal in elaborate detail; feeling the texture of its hair, looking at its teeth and bones and, most of all, marveling at the wonder of its gracefully curved antlers.

Horns, as they grew on cows and bulls, were familiar to me. But antlers were something entirely different — harder, more graceful and certainly more dangerous looking. I nearly lost my senses when told they were shed and regrown every year. For a while I simply didn’t believe it and only gradually allowed myself to be convinced.

And deer could jump, too, higher than a cow or even a horse. My imagination reeled with stories of these wonderful animals.

“Come on,” I said, “nothing can jump a high-wire fence.” So my host took me to a crossing place and showed where the deer-tracked path led up to a fence then continued on the other side. “Wow, they really can do it. Wait till I tell Mom.”

Next day, after breakfast of deer loin, rich gravy and biscuits, I stood in front of the gun rack, itching to get my hands on a genuine deer rifle and go hunting for these wonderful animals. Already, visions of great stags were dancing through my head.

My dad took the first rifle, a Model 99 Savage in .250 caliber, and my brother selected a shortened .30/40 Krag. Why, I wondered, had he passed over a truly beautiful Model 141 Remington pump-action rifle in .30 Remington in favor of the Krag? Anyway, I liked the pump and was glad I had a chance to use it. But when I was clear of the barn lot and stopped to load the rifle, his motives became clear. Nearly all of the cartridges had a sharp indentation on the primer, meaning they had previously misfired and were now useless. Of the lot, only three had virgin primers, and these I fed into the rifle with the optimism of youth.

Less than an hour later, I “jumped” a deer literally in his bed. He came up so close to me that for a moment I was so startled I almost turned and ran. He was not the stag of my dreams but he did have antlers, perhaps six points, and he could be mine! At first the buck ran away so fast that it looked as though I wouldn’t have time for a shot, but then he did something that still has me wondering. After running dead away for about 100 yards, he spun around and headed right at me. Clearly, he would pass by within a few feet, and even at full tilt I’d have a fairly easy shot.

Closer he came and the rifle was at my shoulder, my teeth clinched against the fearful recoil, eye squinted over the sights.

“Hurry, he’s getting away. Try another shot!”

Then the buck whirled again and headed back at me again! He was passing by close enough to hit with a hoe handle.

Tears streamed down my cheeks. Tears of disappointment, tears of frustration and tears of anger. I’d had a better than fair chance and lost it because of grown-ups who’d palmed off a bunch of useless cartridges on me. On the way back to the house, I tried the last cartridge but like its brethren, it only clicked in dismal failure.

It started with a deer rifle that wouldn’t fire and a .22 that missed crows, and I’m still at it, studying, asking questions and, bit by bit, unraveling the puzzles.

As it turned out, I was the only hunter who’d had a “shot” that day, meaning that on the following morning the gun rack was again emptied of all workable deer rifles. All that was left was a little Mossberg Model 151 Rimfire Autoloader complete with a 4X scope (don’t ask how I remember these details, how could I possibly forget?) and several boxes of Super-X ammo.

The day before, I’d passed a newly disked and seeded field of winter wheat that was covered with crows. Surely they would be there again. “If I can’t shoot a deer, at least I’ll shoot some crows,” I told myself as I lifted the .22 from the rack and pocketed a box of ammo.

The crows were there, within easy range, but my first shot kicked up dust far to the left and lower than where I’d aimed. When the crows settled back I missed again the same way. Clearly the rifle didn’t hit where the scope aimed. Why? The rest of the day, and the days following, were spent unraveling the mysteries of sight adjustment and bullet trajectory. A whole new world of excitement lay before me. So many things to learn about guns and only a lifetime to study them.

It started with a deer rifle that wouldn’t fire and a .22 that missed crows, and I’m still at it, studying, asking questions and, bit by bit, unraveling the puzzles.

A small boy can do worse than go deer hunting, even with a rifle that won’t work.

Every time I look at the 12-point whitetail mounted on my trophy room wall, I wonder if I’d do it over again if I had the chance.

It was December ’77 and I was after big whitetails on the Guajolota (translates to female turkey) Ranch in deep south Texas. When I say big whitetails, I don’t mean just big, but big-big, Texas-big, the kind of big that makes vaqueros (cowboys) whisper “muy grande” in wide-eyed wonder. The Guajolota is a working cow ranch but, like most big spreads in south Texas, it swarms with quail and so many big-antlered whitetails that owner Jim McAllen got the idea that he could make more money “farming” deer than beef.

So true to his stock-breeding tradition (McAllen, Texas, is named after Jim’s pioneer family), he set out to make his herd of deer bigger and better by using the same selective breeding techniques proven in the development of superior beef herds. In Texas, just about everyone who hunts deer either owns land, leases hunting rights or hunts on a “pay per day” ranch. (That “per day” arrangement is not the same sort of operation as the exotic game ranches, which also flourish in Texas.) Accordingly, McAllen figured that if he could breed a “super” race of elk-headed whitetails, hunters would just naturally pay more to hunt on the Guajolota.

The first step in his program was to kill off the “culls” — bucks with skimpy antlers and a tendency to pass on this trait — and save the giant bucks for a while for breeding. The program had been in effect only a few years when I hunted the Guajolota, but signs of its success were abundant on my first morning of hunting.

Accompanied by my pal Jim Nolen, maker of the well-known Nolen knives and guided by Ed Dutch, who at that time was the ranch’s game biologist but has since become a top wildlife photographer, we hid under a mesquite tree where we could look out over a 60-yard flat of open grassland.

With a bit of imagination, you might call the south Texas terrain “brush country,” but it’s not the kind of brush hunting one gets in, say, Pennsylvania or Missouri. Just about everything that grows wild in that part of the Texas empire either sticks, scratches bites or poisons, so stalking deer through the cactus and catclaw isn’t all that much fun. That’s why hunting is usually done from a quick stand or from a high seat that lets you look over the thorny chaparral. Fortunately, there is a high buck-to-doe ratio that makes the bucks especially aggressive and eager to challenge other bucks for available does.

The sound of these bucks doing battle is a distinctive clicking and rubbing of antlers that can be heard a pretty fair ways and has the effect of calling other bucks to join the fray. If you ever happen to come upon a couple of bucks fighting it out over some does, you’ll probably spot one or two more waiting their turn, and while the fighting is going on, a smarter-than-average Romeo may be trying to make off with the harem.

Many years ago, some deer hunters had the clever idea of banging a couple of deer antlers together to imitate the sounds of a fight and thereby call bucks to the gun. It worked like a charm and “rattling” up bucks has become an accepted form of the hunting arts.

I’ve tried rattling bucks from Maine to California but the only places I’ve had much success were in areas of dense deer population where there were plenty of aggressive bucks. South Texas is the home of rattling, with both the terrain and temperament of the bucks ideally suited for the technique. The trick, though, in addition to knowing how to rattle the antlers together, is finding a stand that gives you a fairly good view of at least an acre or so of relatively open space.

Some bucks apparently lose all reason at the sound of a fight and dash right in where at any other season they would fear to tread. Some rattlers report having snorting bucks right in their laps after only a moment or two of clicking the antlers. Wiser bucks will come in more cautiously, perhaps circling the stand, wanting to get sight or wind of the combatants. Thus, if you position yourself on the edge of a clearing, you get to see the deer before he gets too close. This also gives the deer a bit of breathing room so he won’t have to get too close and overly spooky. You’ll see deer heads poking out of the bush around the clearing, ears forward, and too curious — or determined — to bound away. More often than not, there’s time for a well-aimed shot, but be sure to keep your rifle close to your shoulder and ready to fire. If they see you move, they’re gone in a flash. Man, deer or fowl, there’s something about poaching on another’s territory that makes any male more than a little spooky.

Greed had slithered to the surface of my consciousness. Greed, unbelievable, unforgiveable greed.

I settled back against the forked trunk of the mesquite tree with my rifle resting on my knees. It was a trim little .250/3000 bolt gun stocked by Don Allen and built on a Mauser action that had been shortened a full inch by ace metalsmith Ron Lampert. Nolen, who was to take first turn playing the antlers, was just to my right and Dutch, who wanted some pictures, was a few yards behind, manning a telephoto lens.

Results were almost immediate. Nolen had banged the antlers no more than twice, twisting and rubbing them together to make the characteristic scrape-click-scrape sound of fighting deer when there, right in front of me, snorting and stomping his feet, was the biggest whitetail buck I’d ever seen on the hoof. He was huge, with perfectly symmetrical antlers. The main beams seemed to grow straight out in a horizontal line before hooking in at the tips. His points stood straight up like rods in an iron gate and the whole picture was a deer-hunter’s fantasy. The buck of a lifetime, too big to be true, perfect. It had to be a lie, a tale told in a deer camp, vividly remembered.

But he was there, stomping, snorting, beautiful. All I had to do was put the crosshairs on his chest and touch the trigger and my whitetail-hunting days would be over, for never would I see a bigger buck. For long moments, I held the crosshairs on his chest, poised to shoot, listening for the click of Dutch’s camera, Click-click-click it went. Now I had a record of the moment, a deer hunter at the gates of paradise. Every nerve in me howled “pull the trigger, pull the trigger,” but I didn’t.

Greed had slithered to the surface of my consciousness. Greed, unbelievable, unforgiveable greed. “Look old boy,” it said to me, “this is only the first deer. Think about the really big ones that are waiting back there in the thicket. We’ve got lots of time to wait for the absolute world beater.”

Incredibly, I lowered my rifle, worked the bolt and emptied the chamber. Then, settling the crosshairs back on the buck’s chest, I tickled the trigger.

“Just wanted to know what it felt like to pull the trigger on a giant buck,” I explained to an absolutely astonished Jim Nolen.

“Waiting for something bigger,” I allowed.

“That’s as big as they get,” was his answer, and I knew greed had done me in.

That morning we rattled in a couple more trophy-size bucks, but nothing nearly so grand as the first, so I couldn’t bring myself to raise the rifle. That afternoon, after a lunch of chili and frijoles served on a tortilla, cowboy-style, followed by a siesta, we tried again — but the antlers were cold and nothing answered the challenge.

That evening a few of McAllen’s vaqueros stopped by the bunkhouse for cerveza and conversation. “It is true,” they asked, “you had El Macho Grande in your sights and did not shoot? Why?”

I really couldn’t answer, but one thing for sure, if I ever saw him again I would shoot.

Next day the antlers were still cold, so by midafternoon we changed tactics and climbed into a tower where we could watch for deer crossing a narrow sendero (a rough, clear-cut roadway). The view from the tower allowed us to look down into the endless thicket, but no deer were moving. By early evening I had counted dozens of javelina, the small wild pigs of the Southwest, and had seen more quail than I thought existed, but no deer other than an occasional doe.

The sun hung low over the deep Texas thicket and a soft haze had wrapped itself around the evening air when the buck stepped into the sendero. The distance was just a bit more than 200 yards, but even with my 7X binoculars, the antlers were hard to judge because the sun was behind the deer, reflecting through the haze so that the deer seemed to be the center of a psychedelic burst of rainbow color. It was not a vision of earth, but a dream in pastel colors with quail calls for background music.

The buck moved slowly, a step at a time, nibbling shoots of greenery. But his antlers remained a mystery. We could see that they were big and exceptionally high, but the way they reflected shafts of gilded light made rational judgment impossible.

“I can’t see his antlers clearly,” Nolen whispered, “but I can see points everywhere.”

The buck was nearly across the sendero now and in a moment he would be gone, perhaps forever. I’d already let the trophy of a lifetime slip through my fingers. Did I dare risk losing a second chance? My trigger finger tightened and the little rifle spoke gently to the soft evening.

The buck was a freak, wearing incredible antlers that had grown to typical, though huge, shape on the right side but with an oddly palmated branch on the left. Is it the trophy of a lifetime, a one-of-a-kind specimen never to be duplicated? Or just a freak with outsize antler growth? I wonder. I wonder every time I look at it on the wall.

In addition to liberal season and bag limits, Alabama has some of the biggest-antlered and heaviest-bodied whitetails I’ve ever looked at. One Alabama trophy deer I saw a few years back got me so excited that I spent several consecutive seasons there trying to bring home the granddaddy.

And I saw lots of bucks, some eight and 10-pointers with such seductive racks that I was often tempted to touch the trigger. Patience prevailed, though, and as days turned to weeks I became more or less accustomed to the sight of the Alabama sun setting over a hardwood thicket in which, from a tree stand, I might be glassing from two to six big-antlered bucks at one time. But as I said, I wanted only the he-coon of the hardwoods and nothing else would do.

How was it, then, that I eventually shot a little eight-pointer?

Hoping to relieve the tedium of my daily wait-and-watch routine, I got myself invited to a party hunt, and on the appointed morning found myself in the midst of an incredible spectacle. The setting was a beautiful Southern mansion complete with curving driveway and vast, oak-bordered lawns. What made the scene so bizarre was the unbelievable variety of humanity strolling or squatting about the neatly clipped grounds. Tweed shooting jackets and English riding boots mixed with faded overalls and run-down clodhoppers while the elegant accents of aristocratic Southern speech were punctuated with the staccato “patoos” of well-aimed tobacco juice. There had been a violent thunderstorm during the night, and judging by the smells of wet wool and soaked leather, many of the attendees had passed the night in the rain.

A metal tub about the size of a horse watering trough was being set up on a stone foundation, eventually to be filled with gallons of cooking oil, and nearby a wild-eyed chap was tugging at a heavy chain leash in a futile attempt to separate two snarling dogs. “Get back,” he yelled when I approached to help, “these dogs are killers.”

“Then why don’t you leave them alone?” I asked.

“I’m trying to keep them from killing each other until Big Bob wakes up.”

“That’s him over yonder,” he responded, waving his free hand in the direction of an inert form stretched out in the tangled remains of what appeared to have once been a rose garden.

I meant to take a closer look, but at that moment a silence fell over the assembly as a spry black man of uncertain vintage, his hair a fluffy white, came down the brick-paved path leading from the big house.

“Mista William is a commin’,” he chanted. “Mista William is commin’, here he come now.”

Sure enough, there was the great one himself, Mister William, owner of thousands of acres of prime farmland and hardwoods, home to the biggest whitetails to be found anywhere. Obviously, Mister William had reached that unique station in society where elegant or even proper attire was no longer required as an emblem of station or success. Accordingly, he was outfitted in soiled chino work pants and shirt, the tail of the latter flapping loosely about his backside, muddied work shoes with, as I remember, only one sock and crowned off with an ancient straw hat that was liberally ventilated with odd-size holes. Yet there was no denying his regal presence. As he puffed unsteadily along the brick pavement, pausing occasionally to scratch, spit or realign his direction, there was a chorus of salutations and more than a few caps were doffed.

“Mornin’ Mista William.” “Fine day Bill.” “Good to see you Mista Bill.”

Each greeting was received with a wave and every face was recognized by name.

“Glad to see you, Jack.” “Nice of you to come over, Pete. How’s Mary and the kids?” “Hi Ralph.”

When at last he faced me, his eyes narrowed, searching for a name.

“Nice to meet you sir. I’m Jim Carmichel and I appreciated the invitation to your deer hunt.”

“Glad to have you, glad to have you,” he gestured grandly. “This hunt ain’t much, just something me and the boys like to do every year about this time.

“Hey there you, Jake, tell Big Bob I said to put Mr. Carmichel here on the road where the deer cross.”

With that he ambled back up the walk, mounted the porch steps and turned to face the breathless assembly. “Boys, the hunt’s on.”

The next few moments were lost in a bedlam of shouts, cheers, running feet and spinning truck tires. Seated in the back of a pickup (I almost made the fatal mistake of climbing into a truck full of savage curs) that fishtailed out of the driveway in a shower of mud and gravel, I caught a glimpse of Mister William as he turned and re-entered the great house, aided by his white-topped butler. Apparently he was not attending his own hunt.

Positioned as I was, on a muddied logging road, I could hear the baying pack of Catahoula curs as they topped a ridge nearly a mile away. As the baying grew louder, it was apparent they were coming my way and would cross the road in front of me. Mister William had indeed given me the best stand on the hunt and in just a few moments I would have a shot.

I was using a borrowed shotgun loaded with No. 000 buckshot and the deer would be crossing from right to left, a dead-easy setup. When the deer broke from cover and bounded across the road, I swung the bead some two feet ahead of his chest and was tightening on the trigger when I realized that it wasn’t much of a buck. An eight-pointer, perhaps, but it was a bucket-head without much width, height, or thickness of beam. The buck certainly wasn’t the world-beater I wanted. With another bound, the young buck disappeared into more timber.

By then the road was covered by a blanket of howling and snarling beasts with their owner, Big Bob, not far behind.

This was the first time I had had a close-up look at Big Bob and he was, to be sure, an awesome apparition. Clad only in bib overalls and a white T-shirt, despite the chill of the day, Big Bob stood a good six or eight inches over six feet and was as wide as a church door. His hair, probably waist length, was knotted behind his head in the style of a samurai warrior, and when he spoke I could see that every tooth in his head was covered in gold. His bout with the rose garden had criss-crossed his arms and face with bloody lacerations, and at his side swung a hunting knife that looked as long as a Saracen scimitar.

As he strode toward me — eyes wild, face blood-caked and mouth flashing of gold — the sword banged against his knee. It was the only weapon he carried. Considering his size, the obvious strength of his hands and arms and the fierceness of his countenance, the knife was more of an affectation than a necessity.

“Where’s the deer?” he asked. “I didn’t hear you shoot.”

“How come? His tracks is right there in front of you.”

At this, his eyes narrowed, “Mister, we ain’t huntin’ trophies, we’re huntin’ meat. We got a lot of people to feed tonight and if you don’t shoot somethin’ these dogs get meaner than they already are.” Big Bob made his point very convincingly.

“The next time something comes by, I’ll be sure to shoot,” I promised.

And that’s exactly what I did. A couple of hours later, the howling pack came by again in violent pursuit of a distinctly undistinguished little eight-pointer.

That evening, my buck and two others that had been killed during the hunt were sliced into bite-size chunks, rolled in batter and deep-fried in the gas-fired horse trough I’d noted earlier.

In time, huge platters were stacked with the delicious-smelling venison tidbits but, for some reason, no one took so much as a single bite. This struck me as curious because no one had eaten since breakfast and I assumed that everyone was as famished as I was. Not wanting to violate local custom, I decided it best not to serve myself until someone else had done so.

The reason for the holdup was soon apparent, however, when Mister William’s butler appeared and announced the immediate arrival of his benefactor. “Here come Mista William, ever’body git ready, here he come now.”

Mister William’s appearance was greatly improved; not only was he better turned out than several hours previous, but his gait was markedly steadier.

Without a word to the hushed onlookers, he marched straight to the deep-fry trough and extracted a crispy brown morsel of batter-dipped venison. For a moment he chewed thoughtfully, eyes cast heavenward. Then, with a sly smile, he made his pronouncement, “Boys, this meat is fit to eat.”

Later, food and drink in hand, I was buttonholed by Big Bob, his countenance no less ominous than earlier and his face still blood-caked from his personal war of the roses.

“If you had shot that other deer,” he allowed, “we would have had some extra meat for my dogs. Now I have to feed ’em dry dog food, which makes their bowels tight and they get meaner than ever.”

“Here,” I answered, handing him my half-emptied plate, “they can have mine.”

This story, “Whitetails I Have Known,” appeared in the September 1982 issue of Outdoor Life.

#8216. The 7 Most Desperate Things I’ve Done in My Search for Ski Boots That Fit

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Seven states, two countries, three acupuncturists, and one orthopedist later, a skier with hard-to-fit feet found the bootfitter she needed. (Photo: Courtesy Abigail Barronian)

Overview: This first-person essay follows one skier’s years-long search for ski boots that fit, with bootfitters in seven states and two countries, a visit to an orthopedist, three acupuncturists, and a stranger’s garage. It’s a funny account of what hard-to-fit feet can drive a person to do, and a reminder that the right bootfitter can change everything.

In my quest for ski boots that fit, I’ve seen bootfitters in at least seven states and two countries. I’ve visited Evo and REI, small independent shops, local chains, and garages-turned-ski shops. I’ve consulted boot designers, brand reps, professional athletes, and gear reviewers; tried Intuitions, ZipFits, and custom footbeds. I’ve seen one orthopedic doctor, three acupuncturists, and two physical therapists. I’ve stayed up at night thinking about boots, and developed recurring stress dreams about them.

Last season, I was beginning to consider looping in a tarot reader or astrologer. Maybe I needed a psychotherapist, or a priest. Maybe I’d have to just quit skiing. And then, finally, I found my bootfitter. But not before resorting to some questionable behavior along the way. Here are seven desperate things I did in my search for a bootfitter who could solve my ski boot issues.

Every pair of ski boots I wore from ages two through 22 were hand-me-downs from my older brothers. Then I started working in the ski industry. While skiing around Big Sky during a media event, a kind man working for Nordica looked at my feet with a frown.

“What are those?” he asked. I was sliding around in some decade-old size 26.5 monstrosities. He shook his head and invited me to swing by the Nordica headquarters in New Hampshire. There, he measured my feet and sent me off with a pair of 25.5 Nordica Promachines.

Everything changed. Suddenly I was in an aggressive stance, my shins met real resistance, my power transfer improved dramatically. I got a taste of what a good boot can do, shortly before developing a wicked case of tendonitis in my ankles and shins.

After two seasons of excruciating, day-ending pain, I booked an appointment with an orthopedic foot and ankle specialist. I knew my boots were the culprit, and couldn’t be sure a doctor would understand the whole foot-encased-in-rigid-plastic thing. I lugged a giant bag with both my alpine and touring boots into the orthopedic practice and pulled them out for show-and-tell.

The physician kindly assured me he knew what ski boots were, and that I wasn’t dealing with any serious medical issues. I’d have to take my boots back where they belonged.

The owner of Santa Fe’s one dedicated ski shop sized me down yet again, into the stiffest 24.5 he had on hand—a 110 from Fischer. I felt like I was skiing in socks and a vise-grip at the same time, and I lost feeling in my feet on the first lap. Mercifully, he let me return them.

I’d hit the central problem: boots big enough to be comfortable gave me tendonitis, and boots small enough to prevent it gave me bunions and nerve pain. So I took my boots to Taos Bootdoctors, where a whole team of bootfitters worked patiently to expand the forefoot. I’d ski for a day or two and come back, over and over, looking for just a few more millimeters. I brought six-packs and did my best to be charming, and the lovely staff never made me feel less important than the tourists dropping thousands of dollars on gear. Still, I couldn’t finish a day without pain.

I soldiered through the season, eyeing an upcoming hut trip with dread. I could manage shorter tours, but a week of daylong missions posed some real problems. Once we were in the mountains, I knew no amount of bunion donuts and anti-inflammatories would save me. I had to instate boots-off breaks in the middle of eight-hour ski days, carefully pulling my socked feet out of jail and propping them up on a backpack in the snow while my friends took an extra lap. Sweet, stupid relief.

Finally, I heard a rumor about a man in Seattle working out of his garage who was willing to do unorthodox things to ski boots. He had a history of custom-fitting plug boots for ski racers, which seemed like a good sign. While visiting family in Washington, I brought him both pairs of boots.

He looked at my feet, listened patiently, and rattled off a comprehensive plan that involved several devices I’d never seen before. Overnight, he molded both pairs into a completely new shape. I never had to touch either boot again, and proceeded with great pleasure to ski 12-hour days in the backcountry and endless resort laps with happy feet. I had found him—the bootfitter I was looking for. Then, he retired.

When my touring boots started to go, I bought a replacement pair and nobody could make them fit. The experience began to take on mythic proportions. I felt like the princess with a pea beneath her many mattresses, or an ugly stepsister trying to cram her foot into a crystal slipper: all discomfort and wrong fit.

It seemed my trusty Tecnicas were the problem. I tried on every touring boot at ski shops in three states. I ordered over a dozen pairs online, obsessively double-checking return policies and momentarily racking up a very scary credit card bill. Eventually, I came crawling back to my old Tecnicas with no plan, two full seasons into the search.

I hesitated to say yes to ski trips, afraid I’d have to sit out ski days because of pain or busted gear. Eventually, it happened: I took my tired old touring boots to Rogers Pass in B.C. and, on day three, broke the upper cuff clean off the bottom section of the boot. Thankfully we were just a few hundred yards from the truck. I spent the entire day sitting at the trailhead.

In the meantime, my alpine boots had begun to warp. I found a replacement pair and was back at square one: home in New Mexico, with two pairs of ski boots that didn’t fit, rapidly dwindling patience, and no bootfitter.

I considered that this might be the end of the road for me as a skier. Then, I learned that one of the best skiers I know had been contemplating quitting the sport because of foot pain. He’d even gone so far as to teach himself to snowboard. But then he found exactly what I’d been looking for: yet another fit-obsessed industry veteran working out of his garage.

I visited another home workshop in western Washington and the bootfitter listened carefully as I explained the issue. Then, he overhauled both pairs of boots, tirelessly stretching the forefoots to give my feet room to breathe. They took on a completely new shape: generous and wide. I took both pairs out for a spin and sighed in relief.

There are a lot of great bootfitters out there. But for a freak like me, I’ve learned I need something of a mad scientist. If you’re plagued with bone spurs, high insteps, wide feet—there’s hope, I promise. With a little faith, a lot of persistence, and maybe something like divine intervention, I trust you’ll find the bootfitter you need. Let’s just hope they don’t retire.

#8211. The Glacier Died—And the Trail Runners Started Coming

I’m standing with Samuel Mendoza on top of Chacaltaya Mountain, 17,785 feet above sea level. Under our feet is a sharp slope of scree, a jumbled descent of rocks with patches of snow. The air is thin, and the vast Bolivian landscape surrounds us.

Directly ahead, the Altiplano—the high plain—stretches from the foot of the mountain. El Alto, the chaotic concrete and red brick city that has grown to roughly 900,000 people, lies at the far edge of the plain at 13,000 feet of elevation, crammed against a canyon’s edge. About 1,500 feet below and connected by a series of cable cars, La Paz, Bolivia’s seat of government, sprawls.

Behind us rises the Huayna Potosí massif. The nearly 20,000-foot summit towers above, its glaciated peak passing in and out of fast-moving clouds. About 45 miles to the northwest, Lake Titicaca—the central motif to Inca creation stories—shimmers on the horizon.

It’s here, on this high mountain of almost-bare rock cradled in the Andes, that Mendoza learned to ski.

Located roughly 20 miles north of La Paz, Chacaltaya was once the world’s highest-altitude ski resort. It began in the 1930s when Raúl Posnansky, an engineer and ski enthusiast, recognized the mountain’s potential, according to 2023 reporting by “Radio Ambulante.” Chacaltaya’s glacier, though relatively small in area at roughly 55 acres, was a solid tongue of ice descending the slope. Temperatures up high stayed low, and snow fell heavily and often during the wet season. The ice was there, had always been there, and would always be there, by all indications at the time.

Posnansky worked to materialize his skiing fantasy: He hired laborers to build an access road, haul materials, construct cabins, and install the first rope tow at Chacaltaya—powered by a truck engine housed in a cabin hanging over the base of the ski run.

Posnansky, along with other mountain athletes, founded the Club Andino Boliviano, a group of dedicated skiers and enthusiasts. To fund the growing ski scene, the club drew involvement from La Paz’s middle and upper classes, and Posnansky and the club persuaded Bolivia’s Congress to pass tax legislation dedicating 1% of the country’s hotel revenue to Bolivia’s Ski and Mountaineering Federation. This funding would help transform Chacaltaya from a passion project into the hub of Bolivian skiing—a hub that, while retaining its roughshod, backyard roots, would grow to host a national ski team, crowded weekend races, the first South American ski championships, and athletes who would represent the country at Winter Olympics.

When Mendoza was a young boy in El Alto, his family wasn’t connected to La Paz’s urban elite who would drive across the Altiplano to ski. Mendoza’s father, however, worked as the caretaker of Chacaltaya, often living for weeks at a time at the resort to maintain the facilities.

When he was 15, Mendoza accompanied his father to the mountain for the first time. He spent his first night at the base racked by altitude sickness.

“My dad gave me coca leaf tea,” he says. The next day, “the sun came out; I felt better. I got acclimated, and I learned to ski.”

Fifty years later, standing once again on the summit, Mendoza is transported back to the resort’s heyday.

“The rope would drop us off here,” he says. “And then …” He puts his hands on bent knees and waves them back and forth in a slalom. He raises his hands over his head and lets out a high yell, feeling the old rush of racing in the cold air.

Mendoza is in his 60s now. He has a harder time seeing, looking out through thick glasses, and his knees sometimes bother him.

Around us the glacier has completely vanished, leaving behind only a mountain of rock.

Infatuated with the world of snow and slopes, Mendoza learned to ski on gear borrowed from Club Andino. He worked long, physical days with his father, tasks ranging from construction and upkeep to manning the rope tow—including rebraiding the wire cable whenever it snapped, a job that left Mendoza with thin white scars across his fingers. From his father, he learned to manage the mountain, the two often sleeping in the lodge for weeks at a time.

Meanwhile, his love for skiing only deepened. Mendoza remembers Stanley Shepard, an American diplomat posted in Bolivia, who taught him advanced techniques and shared the joy of the mountain.

“Stan would drive up this road so fast,” he says as we drive the same route from the city to Chacaltaya some 50 years later. He smiles with the memory of the adrenaline rush.

Mendoza’s ski story exists in a split reality: In one, he is the caretaker’s son, surrounded by a country’s elites who lived near, but not next to, families like his. The socioeconomic divide paralleled the geography: La Paz’s wealthy neighborhoods in the valley, El Alto on the cold outcropping of the Altiplano above. Despite the divide, Mendoza was a vital member of the Chacaltaya scene; the members of Club Andino were his friends. The nights were full of music whenever others would sleep alongside him and his father at the refugio. The period is marked in Mendoza’s mind by shared meals in the cabin and shared runs on the mountain.

By the 1970s, with Chacaltaya entering its golden period, Mendoza was both employee and skier. He tells me he used to set up for the weekend slalom races—ones he’d often compete in as well. I ask about the slalom poles, curious about infrastructure. He tells me they were made nearby. “But the first times,” he says, “we used hollow canes, like cornstalks.”

In a 1976 article in Ski Magazine, American writer Jeff Frees described his visit to the ski hill. There were some two dozen weekly skiers sharing the piste and “a slightly doglegged swath of snow” that was “lined with rocks from top to bottom,” although there were no lift lines, he writes.

The chalet, perched on a rocky precipice, was “so frightening and insecure-looking,” that “some skiers refused to enter it,” Frees says. With the altitude nearing 18,000 feet, other visitors didn’t even bother trying, exiting the minibus up from La Paz only to climb into the truck heading back down the road.

This was the electric, eclectic golden period. One 1,000-foot run served by a single rope tow prone to snapping and powered by a truck engine. A handful of foreign visitors and the dedicated group of Club Andino members. A small, warm refugio built on a cliffside, filled with coca tea, quinoa soup, and music. Weekend races and training events for young locals, supporting ski teams who would go on to participate in four consecutive Olympics starting in 1980. And behind this incredible scene was Samuel Mendoza.

“It was frozen all the time,” Mendoza says. “The people said, ‘This is forever. It will never recede.’”

“But little by little, it started to thaw.”

Scientists had been documenting Chacaltaya for decades, but a systematic study of the glacier began in 1991, led in part by Edson Ramírez of the Universidad Mayor de San Andrés in La Paz (UMSA). Glaciologists’ observations began to echo the concerns skiers had voiced for years: Chacaltaya was melting—and fast.

“Snow would fall at night,” Mendoza says, “but it would be gone by midday.” As temperatures rose, the glacier retreated, exposing more and more of the rock underneath.

While the retreat was evident in some of the earliest photos from the 1940s, Ramírez and his team found that, in just six years from 1992 to 1998, the glacier’s melt had accelerated dramatically, losing more than 40% of its surface area and roughly two-thirds of its ice volume. The team’s prediction: The glacier would disappear within 10 to 15 years.

By 2009, the glacier was completely gone.

“The entire glacier of the world’s highest ski slope had turned to water,” Mendoza reflects.

As the ski run melted under them, various last-ditch efforts were implemented to keep the sport alive. Artificial snow production was attempted, but ultimately proved too costly. Moving the resort to other nearby mountains was considered, but transportation and access were constant hurdles. Even traditional Andean rituals were offered to the mountain gods.

But the glacier, once gone, would not come back.

Without their ski hub, the Club Andino eventually unraveled. A photo hangs in the abandoned refugio of smiling members piled outside the club. Mendoza tells me their names—a running list of friends moved abroad or passed away. Even their headquarters in La Paz is now shuttered.

While sooner than expected, Chacaltaya’s glacier death was not unique within the broader scope of Andean glaciers. Research published in 2026 by Giuliana Adrianzen and Andrew Malone of the University of Illinois Chicago found that Bolivia’s Cordillera Real lost a stunning 42% of its glaciated area between 1992 and 2024.

This trend is widespread across the Andes, which are home to 99% of the world’s tropical glacier area—particularly vulnerable ice fields located near the Earth’s equator.

Glaciers in this latitudinal band are much more susceptible to small temperature changes than those outside of it. Kept frozen primarily by extreme altitude, tropical glaciers already exist close to the temperature threshold to sustain permanent ice; they also don’t experience the long, cold winters of glaciers nearer the poles. Andean glaciers are now thinning 35% faster than the global average, according to a 2025 international report co-authored by researchers at the University of Sheffield. As global warming pushes the freezing level higher, more precipitation falls on these glaciers as rain instead of snow, accelerating the melt.

Over the 60 years between 1960 and 2020, Peru lost 56% of its glacier area. In 2024, Venezuela was declared glacier-free with the death of the Humboldt Glacier (named, perhaps ominously, after the German naturalist who pioneered the notion that everything in the natural world is connected). Colombia is following the same trajectory, having lost more than 90% of its glaciated area since the mid-1800s.

According to UNESCO, the Andes could lose 78 to 97% of their tropical glacier volume by the year 2100.

Of course, more than skiing is at risk—including the water supply risk of some 90 million people across the Andes. These glaciers serve as water reserves for the millions of people who live downstream, and their disappearance foreshadows looming ecological disasters. Many Andean municipalities also rely on hydroelectric power, which depends on steady dry-season meltwater from the glaciers. As the glaciers shrink, that flow is dwindling, increasing the severity of droughts.

While Chacaltaya’s lift has long since stopped spinning, a handful of trained guides and foreign clients continue to practice ski mountaineering in Bolivia, climbing high peaks and bombing descents on still-intact glaciers. While the chalet has ceased to function, the mountain remains an active scientific base. The Chacaltaya Observatory, run by UMSA’s Laboratory for Atmospheric Physics—with multiple international collaborators—continues to measure the atmosphere, climate, and cosmic rays.

And although skiing has abandoned the mountain, Mendoza has not.

Since his father died on Chacaltaya over 30 years ago, Mendoza has served as the mountain’s main caretaker, a position he continues to hold. He spends more time in El Alto with his family now, but he and his brother Adolfo still make multiple trips a week to Chacaltaya, welcoming the handful of tourists who come to visit the abandoned chalet or use it as an acclimatization hike. With the small collected entrance fees, he pays for repairs and maintains his memories of the resort.

Many of Mendoza’s days, however, are spent in solitude, standing alone at 17,000 feet on Chacaltaya’s rocky remains.

“When you’re alone it’s a little sad,” he says. “With only the birds, the condors, the Andean foxes.”

Since the collapse of the glacier, a new group of athletes has taken to Chacaltaya: trail runners—whose arrival is directly tied to skiing’s disappearance. Paolo Choque is the director of skyrunning for the Bolivian Ski and Mountaineering Federation. One of the “last people to learn to ski in Bolivia,” Choque witnessed the collapse of skiing at Chacaltaya, and he has since helped cultivate trail running to take its place.

In 2001, when Choque learned to ski, the main chunk of the glacier was already “ruined,” he says. Against the backdrop of the dying mountain, Choque became involved in promoting skiing and snowboarding in Bolivia, including searching for alternative mountains to host competitions.

In 2011, the federation found another suitable slope at nearby Charquini and hosted a Bolivian Ski Championship. Choque says that snowboarding grew in popularity over a handful of years with the promotion efforts, but participation numbers remained low—with just 25 racers in the snowboard event in 2015. Amid melting ice and low participation, he made the decision to pivot. “I said, ‘No, this isn’t going anywhere. We don’t even have a ski slope.’”

Inspired by the sport’s explosion in Spain, Choque organized a pilot skyrunning race on Chacaltaya in 2016, which was met with a strong reception. Athletes had returned to the mountain. The federation’s championship now draws about 200 participants each year, according to Choque. Racers gain points at multiple events across the country, which take place over otherworldly terrain—from the world’s largest salt flats in Uyuni to the folds of the Sajama stratovolcano, the shores of Lake Titicaca, and, of course, Chacaltaya Mountain.

“Skiing may have died,” Choque says, “but mountain sports have not.”

While private trail races have also increased in popularity in Bolivia over the past decade, the federation aims to develop skyrunning and its next generation of athletes through accessible competition. Race entries, Choque emphasizes, are kept inexpensive, and youth competition categories give athletes the opportunity to qualify for international competition.

“For me, sport must come first, and it must be accessible to everyone,” Choque says.

Despite challenges with funding, Choque says the federation has seen success in sending participants to compete in the South American Championships, where they have earned podium finishes, including three medals in 2025.

As one sport fades and another grows, Choque defines what success could look like for Bolivian skyrunning.

“What I want to achieve is to bring a South American championship here, and if possible, even a youth world championship to Bolivia,” he says. “We have the potential.”

Paolo and the federation hope that Chacaltaya will continue to be an important mountain hub for decades to come—with or without the glacier.

For all of the uniqueness of Chacaltaya’s history, it does mirror a larger global skiing trend: most of the participants were wealthy. Mendoza remembers well the divide caused by the cost of equipment. “From the city of El Alto there weren’t a lot of skiers,” he says.

Through the Ski and Mountaineering Federation, Choque is determined that the next iteration of Chacaltaya’s mountain sports—trail and sky running—do not follow the same pattern. Mendoza, meanwhile, has seen some of the runners who are taking to the mountain to train where he once skied. I ask him if he would ever run one of the races, and he tells me he enjoys running. His knees, though, keep him from doing too much of it. But when a German tourist wanted to race from the summit to the lagoon below, Mendoza happily said yes.

“Replacing skiing at Chacaltaya in the future is possible,” he says.

Looking across the dry slope where he learned to ski, the rusted remains of his rope tow, the faded chalet and the memories contained, Mendoza takes a deep breath. At the end of the day, as we drive the winding dirt road down to the city with Chacaltaya shrinking into the distance behind us, he looks ahead.

“It makes me happy when people visit the mountain,” he says.

#8203. We Tested Handgun Safes To Find the Best for Any Pistol

For home storage of multiple handguns, the Hornady 2-Handgun Keypad Vault Safe is the best overall pick. For securing a pistol in a vehicle, the Steelhead Outdoors Fast Access Pistol Box is the strongest option. For biometric access, the Vaultek DS5i Smart Station leads the category. For bedside access, the RPNB Mounted Safe is the top choice.

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more

Every firearms owner can use a quality handgun safe as a secure storage solution. Aside from providing anti-theft protection, these safes keep pistols and other small valuables and documents from falling into the wrong hands. Additionally, they’ll help protect your investment, especially if you’ve invested thousands into a high-quality handgun.

The smaller footprint also makes handgun safes great for a little extra security in vehicles or RVs that usually lack these types of features. The only hard part is picking the right gun safe for your specific needs. To help you choose, we researched and tested some of the most popular options from Hornady, Liberty, Vaultek and more. After hours of use, these are the best handgun safes available today, according to our experts.

This Hornady handgun safe is incredibly useful for more than just firearms storage. You can adjust the interior shelf to customize your space and the smaller footprint is the perfect size to tuck away in a closet or hide just about anywhere in the house. Because of the 30-minute fireproof rating, this is a solid choice for storing important, irreplaceable documents. There’s enough room inside to store that stuff along with multiple handguns and ammunition.

With a sturdy 16-gauge steel construction, it’s also a tough safe. Most thieves won’t be likely to put in the effort to pry this safe open, especially if you bolt it to the floor using the included hardware. While we wish the battery life was a little better on the electronic lock, it has a keyed lock as backup.

It’s cheaper than a lot of other safes of its quality. It retails for around $250 on Hornady’s website, but you can often find it on sale for under $200. That’s an excellent value considering the size and construction of the safe.

While leaving a firearm or other valuables in a vehicle is never ideal, the Steelhead HD pistol box made me feel a whole lot better about it. Burglars will need to contend with some incredibly thick 12-gauge steel—and that’s only if they somehow get it loose from the ¼-inch galvanized steel security cable. Most smash-and-grab thieves likely won’t put in the effort required to get this one loose. Even if they do, they’ll have a hell of a time opening it. I slammed it on the ground multiple times trying to pop it open. I only succeeded in making the exterior dirty.

While there’s only one entry method via a key, it’s a secure lock. And the paperwork I got with the safe indicates each key is unique because it requires a new cylinder and keys if you lose both. That means someone can’t simply buy one of these safes and have a magic key to every Steelhead box out there. That’s a nice little extra peace of mind.

The $170 price point is expensive, but it’s also understandable once you hold this safe in your hands. I feel like this thing would shrug off being run over by a tank. I didn’t think products of this quality were made anymore. Bonus: This box is even TSA-approved for flying. Given the way the interior foam cradled securely and protected my Glock 19, I wouldn’t worry about baggage handlers being rough with it.

The Vaultek Smart Station is an incredibly cool piece of tech because it’s secure storage that just also happens to double as a piece of multi-functional furniture. This gives the safe fast, single-handed access via the biometric fingerprint scanner. We doubt thieves will think this is just a clock radio due to the size. But Vaultek didn’t skimp on the anti-theft protection details. This pistol safe is built from a rugged 18-gauge steel. You can also tether it to the wall via a security cable.

It’s a great bedside safe that’s perfect for emergencies. But at the same time, it serves as both an LED clock and a charging station for smart phones. While it has a wireless charger, Vaultek also placed some charging ports on the back for phones without that feature.

The only downside of this safe is that it’s expensive. But considering the high cost of handguns, the investment is worth it. There also aren’t many other safes that look this nice while offering this many features. This safe even monitors the interior temperature and humidity, ensuring your firearm won’t rust, and connects to a smart phone so you can easily manage authorized users.

This safe is designed to be mounted vertical on the side of a nightstand or under a desk with a handy bracket. We feel like it also has potential for some vehicles if you can find a large enough space. Either way, it doesn’t immediately look like a gun safe, which means it might be overlooked by a thief checking the obvious locations in a bedroom. We like the incredibly fast lock RPNB put on this safe. It doesn’t matter if you buy the keypad only version or the biometric version. Both are very fast, popping open immediately. That makes it ideal for emergencies, especially while you are sleeping. And RPNB made it possible to program over 50 fingerprints, so every adult in the home can have access while keeping kids safe.

The price for this safe is great, too. The keypad-only version is $69.99 while the biometric version is $109.99. However, this isn’t a standalone safe. You will need to permanently screw it into a piece of furniture or a wall for it to be effective. We recommend using a large, sturdy nightstand or desk because it weighs nearly 8 pounds.

While determining the best handgun safes, we evaluated the anti-theft protection features of each safe, along with additional security features like a security cable for vehicles. We looked at the construction and overall footprint of each safe to determine a best use scenario for each of them.

We also did hands-on testing with some of the safes. This allowed us to assess the locks and determine how quickly the different modes of access work. Although most safes aren’t likely to see a lot of abuse unless a burglar is trying to break into it, I also did a little durability testing. This involved dropping the safes on the ground to see if they would scratch or pop open accidentally. Thankfully, the safes I tested passed with flying colors.

Additionally, we considered the following factors:

Access Methods: Does this safe utilize mechanical keyed locks, number locks, or the latest in biometric locks? Are there backup access features?

Profile: How well does the safe tuck away in a closet or drawer? Is the safe slim enough to tuck under a car seat?

Value: Does the price point of the safe appropriate considering the features and construction?

When it comes to buying a gun safe, most people are going to be looking at the cost, capacity, and access methods. But it’s also important to consider where you plan to put the safe. A safe that fits into a drawer is different from one that’s designed to tuck under a car seat. Consider how accessible the safe will be, especially if you need to get into it at a moment’s notice.

When you’re trying to determine what size gun safe you need, think about where you’ll use it (see above) and how many pistols you have to store. If you’re looking for a handgun safe that’s portable or can fit in your car, you’ll likely need something smaller and more compact than a safe you set up at home. A good rule of thumb is to buy a safe that’s a little bit larger than your current firearms collection, as you may end up adding a gun (or two or three) later on down the road.

Is the safe water-resistant or waterproof? What about fire-resistant or fire-proof? While most safes are built to be tough and durable, some hold up to the elements better than others. Look for a pistol safe that’s made of at least 11- or 12-gauge steel with tight-fitting seals to keep out moisture and smoke.

Most modern safes have one of three ways to provide access to firearms: keyed locks, electronic locks with a keypad, or biometric locks. Some safes use more than one so there is a backup access method in case you lose the keys or forget the code.

Biometric safes are the preferred mode if you want quick access. Most will pop the safe open in only a second or two. It’s much easier to open one of these safes than turning a key or punching in an access code in an emergency, although you need to be vigilant and ensure the batteries are fresh for any electronic lock to work properly. Access modes are largely personal preference based on what each gun owner feels will be most secure for their needs.

Depending on the type of safe you want or need, gun safes can vary greatly in terms of price. Smaller lock boxes can start under $50, while higher end larger safes can cost a few hundred dollars. Know your budget before you start shopping so you can narrow down your search accordingly.

Handguns can rust in a safe if proper precautions are not taken. It is not advisable to mount a safe in a garage or other environment that isn’t carefully climate controlled, especially if it’s humid. However, you can safeguard your pistol safe against rusting problems by adding some silica gel packs to absorb any extra moisture.

The best area for a gun safe is a climate-controlled part of the home where firearms won’t be prone to rusting. Other than that, it’s largely personal preference. In the bedroom is a great place for quick and easy access. But it’s also likely to be the first place that burglars check. Putting the safe in other areas of the house makes it harder to find for thieves, but also reduces accessibility in an emergency.

Biometric safes utilize an electronic system as an easier and faster way to unlock the safe. This style of safe is perfect for an emergency because most can open in only a second or two simply by reading the stored fingerprints of the gun’s owner. Most safes of this style make it possible to store multiple fingerprints if you want more than one person to have access.

#8199. Mandatory Race Gear You’ll Actually Want to Use

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Many ultramarathons, including Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB) require runners to carry certain gear. Cade Michael spent years as an unsponsored elite trail runner honing in his mandatory race kit with items that he both genuinely enjoys using and can be found affordably. He did this by taking advantage of sales, buying second-hand, and borrowing from friends. Here he shares his tips for building out your own race kit, including his favorite items in his pack.

Mandatory trail running race equipment is a lot like American health insurance: We all hate it. We’re all tempted to skimp on it. And we all inevitably need it when we’re least prepared. Required gear (or most of it, anyway) doesn’t have to be a waste of money or space. After spending yeas as an unsponsored runner curating my mandatory race gear, here’s my guide to getting gear that you’ll actually want to use more than once every 365 days, including my favorite items in my pack.

UTMB, among other races, often has extensive gear requirements and—whether you like to admit it or not—it’s usually for good reason. Weather and conditions can change rapidly in the mountains, and when you’re pushing your body to the extreme for hours (if not days) on end, as a general rule of thumb, it’s better to have it and not need it than to need it and not have it—particularly for race organizers’ liability insurance.

For example, while it may feel ridiculous for a 100K on the notoriously hot Western States 100 course in Auburn, California to make you carry a rain jacket and emergency blanket, the 2025 Canyons 100K  (on the same trails) saw snow at the start and highs around 40 degrees Fahrenheit. Packing three layers, two pairs of pants, and multiple pairs of gloves might seem like overkill for a day spent backcountry skiing in February, much less a running race in late August, but at the 2025 UTMB, ultrarunning’s most iconic race turned into a game of surviving the winter storm-like conditions.

I know all too well the allure of going light. But much like Admiral Ackbar’s epiphany at the Battle of Endor, it’s (usually) a trap. At the 2026 Twisted Fork Trail Festival in Park City, Utah, weather forecasts changed drastically in the 48 hours leading into race day, projecting relentless freezing rain. I chucked on a pair of gloves and arm sleeves and figured I’d warm up plenty as the race went on. As soon as we hit the first descent I lost feeling in my hands, feet, legs, cheeks, and plenty of other places I won’t call by name. My heart rate plummeted and I struggled for the entire remainder of the day. Eventual women’s champion, Rachel Drake, on the other hand, donned a warm base layer, long tights, gloves, and vest loaded with extras. Drake is an MD/PhD, mom, and professional runner for Nike ACG. Be more like Rachel, and less like me.

But you don’t have to hate the gear you’re going to buy one way or another to participate in these events.

Quality, packable gear can not only serve to save your race should conditions take a turn through the night in the Alps, but it can also save your run or, heaven forbid, life, if you’re spending any time out on the trails. While you could probably get away with using children’s XXS sized Walmart rain pants, your niece’s tiny pinky swim goggles, and Amazon’s finest two dollar headlamp, you can also use the mandatory equipment list of your next ultra as an excuse to get quality gear that won’t sit at the bottom of your junk drawer until next summer.

Here are my tips and tricks for getting good, lasting gear that’s a little easier on your bank account than the race entry fees and international travel.

Required kit, in most cases, isn’t going to be the product you wear holes through everyday. One is built to be versatile, lightweight, and packable while the other is made for a specific purpose and durability. Some pieces of equipment, like your rain coat for UTMB, are ones you want to stand up in the most brutal of conditions. Others, like a secondary headlamp, are areas you might be able to save some weight and cash.

Lightweight, packable gear is usually updated every year just like the rest of a brand’s product line and often goes on sale during off-season months or discount days (ahem, Black Friday or REI member days). A lot of years, the only update is the colorway, so just get the highlighter yellow and own it!

Better yet, buy gear second hand. Many of the products I’ll list below I grabbed from resale sites like Poshmark or Mercari for a fraction of the retail price

It may seem obvious, but always get your size. It might seem worth it to save a few grams and get a women’s XXS when you’re in the Chamonix Arc’teryx store panic-buying a rain jacket 24 hours before the gun goes off, but I promise you it’s not. Get the extra ounce and future you will be proud of the responsible decision to get something you’ll actually put on your body.

If you’re questioning whether a piece of gear will satisfy the requirements set by race organizers for your next ultra, err on the side of caution. Get the marginal gains wherever you can within reason, but I promise you trimming two centimeters off your bandaging or emergency blanket will not make Col du Grand Ferret any easier or quicker.

People in your run club and or training partners have probably raced an ultra and used this stuff before. If it’s not something you will need time and time again, it’s OK to borrow it; chances are, they won’t need it in the next week or two anyway. The more you share, the more you save.

Get familiar with your equipment. Try it in training, just like you would a pair of shoes or a nutrition product. Being able to mindlessly locate and use your gear will pay dividends when you have no mindfulness left late into an ultra. Brand-spanking-new isn’t always best.

If you’re between two rain jackets, just get the one with the extra zipper. The best gear is the gear you use. Ruth Croft and Tom Evans won a historically cold and wet UTMB in 2026. When they bundled up through the night, I’m certain they were rocking the clothes they trusted to get the job done, not the ones that came in a few grams under. You’re racing an ultra marathon through the mountains, not a 5K parkrun.

Please keep reading, my opinions are important. Seriously though, whether it’s one of our gear roundups (shameless plug) or your favorite YouTuber, people put dozens of pieces through countless miles so you don’t have to. Take a few extra minutes to read a few pros and cons before you pull the trigger.

A lot of thought and stress can go into mandatory equipment, but don’t let it take away from the race experience. At my first UTMB race, UTMB Whistler in Canada, the cold-weather gear policy was implemented two days before the race due to a snowstorm. I’d just come from racing in California and Spain in September, so I didn’t have a suitcase stocked with skimpy mandatory equipment. Luckily for me, I couldn’t afford to grab a bunch of last-second gear and just used what I had with me. Retrospectively, my pack was a little heavier and bulkier than it could have been had I been properly prepared, but I didn’t think about the weight once during the race. But boy, was I glad to have warm gloves and a beanie that fit.

Here’s a list of some of my favorite mandatory equipment I’ve amassed over a couple of years of racing in Chamonix as an unsponsored athlete.

This one is totally optional and, frankly, probably only applicable for a shorter ultra like MCC or OCC during UTMB week. The mini phone is a great tool to have if you’re only out for a handful of hours. So long as you ensure you get a SIM card that has roaming and data enabled for whatever country or region you will be running through, it can call, text, Whatsapp, and even Strava. UTMB requires you to have a smart phone capable of downloading and using the LiveTrail app, and this Google Play Store enabled pocket rocket is the smallest you can get while satisfying the requirements. It also takes pretty cool retro camcorder-style videos. For the longer races like CCC and UTMB, however, it’s probably your safest bet to just bring along your standard, daily driver smart phone. You have to keep your phone on at all times throughout the race, and the number of charging bricks you’d have to haul to keep this thing running through the night outsizes any weight savings it might provide.

Typically, flasks are flasks. Your running vest will usually come with a couple that fit. That being said, I usually hate running vests. One of the primary reasons is the way traditional flasks sit in the sleeves, bouncing around and uncomfortably rubbing against my collarbone. My pro tip here is to check out flasks with smaller lids like these Hydrapak pocket flasks. Theoretically, they’re made to fit flush with your running belt, but I’ve found they are less bulky and front heavy in a running vest, too. (As long as they fit in the sleeves.)

A sure bet to be on the required kit list for almost any ultra is a waterproof rain jacket. UTMB’s specifications are rather persnickety, with required minimum waterproof rating, breathability score, sealed seams, and an integrated hood. The On Ultra Jacket lives up to demands while remaining paper thin, uber light, and incredibly packable. It can end up feeling a little too trash-baggy and unbreathable to be your workhorse running jacket, but nevertheless it’s a great piece to be able to throw in your pack anytime you head up into the unpredictable weather of the alpine.

For headlamps, I always keep a couple of options hanging around for the varying amount of daylight in different races. For OCC, for example, I opt for the Petzl E+Lite. It’s so small and light it’s an almost imperceptible item to carry and it uses nickel-sized 2432 batteries, but, as you might expect, that means it is useless for anything more than an hour or so in a pinch.

For longer races where you will inevitably be running through hours of darkness, if not the entire night, this is not somewhere to skimp on weight. A popular option in this category is the Petzl Iko Core, which features an incredible 500 lumen bulb, outstanding shine time, and a replaceable battery that sits at the back of the crown for stability. If you’re running UTMB, don’t forget to pick up the mandatory red light filter for fragile wildlife areas.

The crown jewel of mandatory equipment is the running vest. It’s what will hold all of your other mandatory equipment. It’s what will be in direct contact with your body and can make or break the convenience and comfortability of your racing experience. But, most importantly, it’s what will show up in all your post-race photos and make you look either super nerdy or really cool—by which I mean slightly less nerdy. In all seriousness, choosing your hydration vest is critical—and critically personal. Salomon and Nathan offer popular options that have dominated the category dating back to the cradle of civilization. (Hammurabi allegedly kept his chisel in an ADVskin 5L.) But the market is flooding with alternatives as the sport continues to grow, so there is no shortage of options. The most important things to consider are fit and layout. For my preferences, which is for my vest to feel as least like a vest as possible, the Tantrums Crest 6 and Kiprun Pro Team 5L have been excellent. The pocket layouts have tons of nooks and crannies that scratch my obnoxious need for hyperorganization better than keeping foods from touching on my Thanksgiving plate. They have minimal bounce, soft fabric across the shoulder straps, and offer a rear tunnel pocket for an extra flask. Both the Tantrums and Kiprun also come in light colors, a touch that seems a blatant choice for any piece of athletic equipment but was, until recently, a white whale on the hydration vest market.

A good cap is indispensable and obviously extends beyond race day. It’s not that deep, just get one that feels and looks good. Ciele is a sure fire way to fit in at the coolest run club in town.

Waterproof pants can be a tricky one. They’re probably the thing you’ll use the least in everyday training (save for the tinfoil-esque emergency blanket), and they’re one of the most expensive pieces of kit on the list. Getting a pair that satisfies UTMB’s specifications and doesn’t necessitate a 25-liter pack to fit is going to be steep. On makes the Ultra Pant compliment to the aforementioned jacket, but I use these Rab Phantom Pants. The two are kind of “six-one, half-dozen another,” so just grab whichever you can find on a last-season sale.
